title: Big picture
oneLiner: How the services fit into one system: where each one lives, how a request flows through them, and where you secure and connect it. Tap a diagram to see it full size.

notes.text: The whole system on one page

notes.html: One rule: global edge in front, one region behind it, a VPC across two AZs inside, managed services beside the VPC, and a second region for DR. Most exam scenarios are one slice of this picture.

notes.caption: The full production setup. Numbers follow one request. Orange = in-memory cache; dashed = standby or DR.

notes.html: One rule: if it has no region selector it's global, if it runs in your subnets it's in the VPC, and if it's a disk or an instance it's stuck in one AZ. Scope tells you what fails together and what you must copy for DR.

notes.caption: Nested scopes. Orange = AZ-bound things the exam likes to trap you on.

head: Scope
Services
Why it matters / do instead
rows: Route 53, CloudFront, Global Accelerator, IAM, Organizations, WAF on CloudFront
Nothing to copy for DR. WAF on an ALB or API Gateway is regional, though.
S3, DynamoDB, Lambda, SQS, SNS, KMS, Secrets Manager, CloudWatch, API Gateway
Multi-AZ by default. Copy to another region with CRR, Global Tables, multi-Region keys, secret replication.
ALB, NLB, Auto Scaling group, EFS, RDS Multi-AZ pair
Survives one AZ only if you pick subnets in 2+ AZs.
Subnet, EC2 instance, EBS volume, NAT gateway, single RDS instance, ENI
Fails with its AZ. EBS moves AZ by snapshot; NAT needs one per AZ for HA (today AWS also has a regional NAT gateway mode, newer than the exam).

items: S3 bucket names are global, but the bucket and its data live in one region.
A subnet is in exactly one AZ. A VPC spans all AZs in its region, but never two regions.
An EBS volume can only attach to an instance in the same AZ. To move it: snapshot, then create a volume in the new AZ.
One NAT gateway is a single-AZ point of failure for the other AZ's private subnets.
"move an EBS volume to another AZ"
Snapshot → new volume in that AZ
"NAT gateway is a single point of failure"
One NAT gateway per AZ, each AZ routes to its own
Regional web ACL on the ALB

notes.html: One rule: each layer only accepts traffic from the layer in front of it. WAF at the edge, then security groups that name the previous security group as their source, and NACLs on subnets for explicit denies.

notes.caption: Security group chaining. Orange = security group rules, each pointing at the layer before.

Rule
Why

Stops web attacks before they reach your region
443 from the CloudFront managed prefix list

App port from the ALB security group
Instances scale in and out; the rule still holds

notes.html: Today's AWS also offers CloudFront VPC origins, which let the ALB sit in a private subnet with no public access at all. The exam answer is still usually the managed prefix list (or a custom header checked by the ALB).

items: Security groups attach to network interfaces (EC2, ALB, RDS, Lambda in a VPC), not to subnets. Subnets get NACLs.
Security groups are stateful: allow inbound and the reply is allowed. NACLs are stateless: open ephemeral ports 1024-65535 for return traffic.
Security groups have no deny rule. "Block this IP" → NACL deny, or WAF IP set.
"only the web tier can reach the database"
DB SG source = web tier SG

questions.q: A web app runs on one EC2 instance in one AZ. It must survive the loss of an AZ with the least operational overhead. What should the architect do?

options.t: Put an ALB in front of an Auto Scaling group that spans two AZs
options.why: The ALB and ASG are regional; the ASG replaces instances in the healthy AZ automatically.

options.t: Take hourly EBS snapshots and restore in another AZ on failure
options.why: That's backup and restore: manual and slow, not HA.

options.t: Move the instance to a cluster placement group
options.why: Cluster placement packs instances into one AZ, the opposite of what you need.

options.t: Add a second instance in the same AZ behind Route 53
options.why: Both instances still fail with the AZ.

questions.q: Users must reach the app only through CloudFront. Some users hit the public ALB directly. What is the simplest fix?

options.t: Allow inbound 443 on the ALB security group only from the CloudFront managed prefix list
options.why: Only CloudFront's origin-facing IPs can reach the ALB, and AWS keeps the list up to date.

options.t: Add a NACL that denies all IPs except CloudFront's
options.why: CloudFront has many changing IPs; NACLs have a small rule limit. Hard to maintain.

options.t: Move the ALB to a private subnet without any other change
options.why: CloudFront then can't reach it unless you set up VPC origins.

options.t: Enable Shield Advanced on the ALB
options.why: DDoS protection, it doesn't restrict who can connect.

questions.q: Only the app tier, which scales from 2 to 20 instances, may connect to an RDS database. Which rule is most maintainable?

options.t: RDS security group: allow 3306 from the app tier's security group
options.why: SG chaining. New instances carry the app SG, so the rule covers them automatically.

options.t: RDS security group: allow 3306 from each app instance's private IP
options.why: IPs change as the ASG scales; you'd keep editing the rule.

options.t: NACL on the data subnet: allow 3306 from the app subnet CIDR
options.why: Works, but it's coarser (any host in the subnet) and stateless, so you also need return-port rules.

options.t: IAM policy that allows rds:Connect for the app role
options.why: IAM database auth controls login, not which hosts can open a network connection.

questions.q: A security team must block one malicious IP range from reaching instances in a subnet. What should they use?

options.t: A network ACL deny rule on the subnet
options.why: NACLs support explicit deny, evaluated by rule number.

options.t: A security group deny rule
options.why: Security groups have allow rules only.

options.t: Remove the route to the internet gateway
options.why: That cuts off all internet traffic, not one range.

options.t: GuardDuty
options.why: GuardDuty detects threats, it doesn't block traffic.

questions.q: A NACL allows inbound 443 and outbound 443. Web clients connect, but responses never arrive. Why?

options.t: NACLs are stateless; outbound must also allow ephemeral ports 1024-65535 back to clients
options.why: Replies go to the client's ephemeral port, which the NACL blocks.

options.t: Security groups are stateless and need an outbound rule
options.why: Security groups are stateful; replies are allowed automatically.

options.t: The internet gateway blocks return traffic
options.why: An IGW doesn't filter traffic.

options.t: NACL rules are evaluated alphabetically
options.why: They're evaluated by rule number, lowest first.

questions.q: Instances in a private subnet upload large files to S3 through a NAT gateway, and data transfer costs are high. What is the most cost-effective fix?

options.t: Add an S3 gateway endpoint and route the subnet's S3 traffic to it
options.why: Free, stays on the AWS network, and removes NAT per-GB charges for S3 traffic.

options.t: Add an S3 interface endpoint
options.why: Works, but it costs per hour and per GB. The gateway endpoint is free.

options.t: Move the instances to a public subnet
options.why: Exposes them, and it's a security regression just to save money.

options.t: Use S3 Transfer Acceleration
options.why: Speeds long-distance uploads over the internet; it costs more.

questions.q: A Lambda function in a private subnet with no NAT gateway must send messages to SQS. Traffic must not leave the AWS network. What should the architect add?

options.t: An interface VPC endpoint for SQS
options.why: SQS has no gateway endpoint; an interface endpoint gives it a private IP in the subnet.

options.t: A gateway VPC endpoint for SQS
options.why: Gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB.

options.t: An internet gateway
options.why: Private subnets can't use it directly, and it goes over the internet.

options.t: VPC peering with the SQS VPC
options.why: SQS isn't in a VPC you can peer with.

questions.q: Two private subnets in two AZs both route to one NAT gateway in AZ-a. What happens if AZ-a fails, and what is the fix?

options.t: AZ-b loses outbound internet; put a NAT gateway in each AZ and route each subnet to its own
options.why: A NAT gateway lives in one AZ. One per AZ removes the single point of failure.

options.t: Nothing; NAT gateways are regional and fail over automatically
options.why: A standard (zonal) NAT gateway is redundant only inside its own AZ. AWS added a regional NAT gateway mode in Nov 2025, but the exam answer is still one per AZ.

options.t: AZ-b loses outbound; add a second internet gateway
options.why: A VPC has one IGW, and the IGW isn't the problem.

options.t: Nothing; the instances fall back to the internet gateway
options.why: Private subnets have no route to the IGW.

questions.q: An EBS volume in us-east-1a must be attached to an instance in us-east-1b. What should the architect do?

options.t: Snapshot the volume and create a new volume from it in us-east-1b
options.why: EBS volumes are AZ-bound; snapshots live in S3 at region level.

options.t: Detach and attach it to the instance in us-east-1b
options.why: A volume can only attach in its own AZ.

options.t: Enable EBS Multi-Attach
options.why: Multi-Attach is for instances in the same AZ.

options.t: Copy the volume with DataSync
options.why: DataSync moves files between storage services, not block volumes between AZs.

questions.q: Which two services are global and need no copy in a DR region?

options.t: IAM
options.why: Users, roles and policies are global.

options.t: Route 53
options.why: Hosted zones and health checks are global.

options.t: DynamoDB
options.why: Regional; use Global Tables for other regions.

options.t: KMS
options.why: Regional keys; use multi-Region keys to decrypt in another region.

options.t: Secrets Manager
options.why: Regional; replicate secrets to the DR region.

questions.q: An app is served directly by an ALB (no CloudFront). The team needs SQL injection protection. Where does the WAF web ACL go?

options.t: A regional web ACL associated with the ALB
options.why: WAF attaches to ALB, API Gateway, AppSync and Cognito regionally.

options.t: A global web ACL, which only works with CloudFront
options.why: Global web ACLs are for CloudFront; the ALB uses a regional one.

options.t: A security group rule on the ALB
options.why: SGs filter by port and source, they can't inspect SQL.

options.t: Shield Standard
options.why: DDoS protection at layers 3/4, not SQL injection.

questions.q: The RDS primary is overloaded by reads, and Multi-AZ is already on. What should the architect add for read scaling?

options.t: Read replicas, or ElastiCache for hot reads
options.why: Replicas are readable; a cache takes repeated reads off the DB.

options.t: Point reads at the Multi-AZ standby
options.why: The classic Multi-AZ standby isn't readable; it's only for failover.

options.t: A second Multi-AZ standby
options.why: Still not readable; it adds HA, not read capacity.

options.t: A larger EBS volume
options.why: Storage size doesn't fix read CPU load.

questions.q: A company has 30 VPCs and two data centers that must all reach each other. Which option has the least operational overhead?

options.t: Transit Gateway with VPN or Direct Connect attachments
options.why: One transitive hub instead of hundreds of peerings.

options.t: Full mesh of VPC peering
options.why: 435 peerings, plus peering isn't transitive to on-prem.

options.t: PrivateLink between every VPC
options.why: PrivateLink exposes single services, not whole networks.

options.t: A VPN from each VPC to each data center
options.why: 60 VPNs to manage.

questions.q: A SaaS provider must expose one API to hundreds of customer VPCs. Many customers use the same CIDR (10.0.0.0/16). What should they use?

options.t: PrivateLink: NLB in the provider VPC, interface endpoints in customer VPCs
options.why: Only the endpoint's IP is used in the customer VPC, so overlapping CIDRs don't matter.

options.t: VPC peering with each customer
options.why: Peering fails with overlapping CIDRs.

options.t: Transit Gateway
options.why: Overlapping CIDRs break routing.

options.t: Public ALB with IP allow-listing
options.why: Goes over the internet; the question implies private access.

questions.q: A company needs an encrypted link to AWS this week, and a consistent 10 Gbps link long term. What should the architect do?

options.t: Site-to-Site VPN now; order Direct Connect and keep the VPN as backup
options.why: VPN is up in minutes; DX takes weeks. VPN over DX also adds encryption.

options.t: Direct Connect only
options.why: Weeks to provision, and not encrypted by default.

options.t: VPN only, with more tunnels
options.why: ~1.25 Gbps per tunnel over the internet; not consistent.

options.t: VPC peering to the data center
options.why: Peering connects VPCs, not on-prem networks.

questions.q: IPv6 instances in a private subnet must reach the internet for updates but must not accept inbound connections. What should they route through?

options.t: An egress-only internet gateway
options.why: Outbound-only for IPv6, like NAT for IPv4.

options.t: A NAT gateway
options.why: NAT gateways are for IPv4 (plus NAT64 translation), not plain IPv6 egress.

options.t: An internet gateway
options.why: IPv6 addresses are public; an IGW allows inbound too.

options.t: A gateway endpoint
options.why: Only for S3 and DynamoDB, not the internet.

questions.q: A relational database needs an RPO of about 1 second and RTO of about 1 minute across regions. Which option fits?

options.t: Aurora Global Database
options.why: Storage-level replication under a second; promote a secondary region in about a minute.

options.t: RDS cross-region read replica
options.why: Async; lag can be longer and promotion is slower.

options.t: Daily snapshots copied to the other region
options.why: RPO of up to a day.

options.t: RDS Multi-AZ
options.why: Protects against an AZ failure, not a region.

questions.q: S3 objects encrypted with SSE-KMS must be readable in the DR region with the same key after replication. What should the architect use?

options.t: S3 Cross-Region Replication with a KMS multi-Region key
options.why: The replica key has the same key ID and material, so objects decrypt in region B.

options.t: Same-Region Replication
options.why: Stays in one region.

options.t: Copy the KMS key to the other region manually
options.why: Single-region keys can't be exported or copied.

options.t: Switch to SSE-S3 and let AWS handle it
options.why: Loses the KMS key control the scenario requires.

questions.q: A TCP game server runs in two regions. Failover must happen in seconds, without waiting for DNS caches. What should the architect use?

options.t: Global Accelerator with endpoints in both regions
options.why: Static anycast IPs; health checks shift traffic in seconds with no DNS change.

options.t: Route 53 failover routing
options.why: Clients cache DNS until the TTL expires.

options.t: CloudFront with an origin group
options.why: CloudFront is for HTTP(S), not raw TCP game traffic.

options.t: An ALB that spans both regions
options.why: ALBs are regional; they can't span regions.

questions.q: A global user base complains of slow image loads from an ALB in one region. Which change is most cost-effective?

options.t: Put CloudFront in front, with S3 or the ALB as origin
options.why: Edge caching cuts latency and origin load.

options.t: Deploy the full stack in five regions
options.why: Expensive and complex for static images.

options.t: Global Accelerator
options.why: Speeds the network path but doesn't cache; every image still hits the origin.

options.t: Bigger EC2 instances
options.why: The latency is distance, not CPU.
